**Methodological frame.** BlackRock manages client assets rather than holding positions on its own balance sheet. Its 13F-HR (at 31.03.2026: $5.72T, ~50,651 positions; filed 13.05.2026) is CLIENTS' US-listed equities, not the holding company's assets, so the 13F top positions are deliberately absent here. The franchise's "portfolio" is the mix of assets under management (AUM). Balance sheet seed and co-investments in its own funds are disclosed in principle, without a line-by-line breakdown in this cycle (see gaps).

**AUM by product at 31.03.2026 (Q1 2026 earnings release, confirmed line by line):**

| Product | AUM, $m | % of AUM | Q1 base fees, $m | % of base fees | Q1 net flows, $m |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 7,661,385 | 55% | 2,626 | 48% | +71,842 |
| Fixed income | 3,270,863 | 24% | 1,058 | 19% | +34,314 |
| Multi-asset | 1,222,612 | 9% | 381 | 7% | +17,827 |
| Private markets | 320,431 | 2% | 658 | 12% | +9,076 |
| Liquid alternatives | 108,639 | 1% | 197 | 4% | +5,551 |
| Digital assets | 60,671 | 0% | 42 | 1% | +935 |
| Currency & commodities | 176,676 | 1% | 136 | 3% | −3,644 |
| **Long-term total** | **12,821,277** | 92% | 5,098 | 94% | +135,901 |
| Cash management | 1,073,323 | 8% | 340 | 6% | −6,177 |
| **Total** | **13,894,600** | 100% | 5,438 | 100% | +129,724 |

**By investment style (31.03.2026):**

| Style | AUM, $m | % of AUM | Q1 base fees, $m | % of base fees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| iShares ETFs | 5,485,544 | 39% | 2,406 | 44% |
| Active | 3,410,923 | 25% | 2,350 | 43% |
| Non-ETF index | 3,924,810 | 28% | 342 | 7% |

**The economics of the concentration:** ETFs plus non-ETF index (passive) are 67% of long-term AUM but only ~51% of base fees. Active plus private markets is ≈27% of AUM but ~55% of base fees — that is where most of the fee income is generated. iShares is the single most profitable franchise: $5.49T of AUM, $2.41bn of base fees in the quarter. The effective base fee rate on long-term AUM is ≈0.16% a year.

**Private markets sub-classes (NOT confirmed against primary sources).** The FACTS agent gave a split of private credit $147.0bn / infrastructure $111.9bn / private equity $30.2bn / real estate $21.7bn / multi-alts $9.6bn. Those figures are **absent** from the Q1 2026 release and from the earnings call transcript; the release carries only the private markets aggregate of $320,431m and a note that the $9bn of inflows was "led by private credit and infrastructure". Another internal estimate gives conflicting numbers (infra $210bn, private credit $40bn→$111bn). Both splits are flagged as unconfirmed — see gaps.

**Q1 2026 geographic flows (long-term net flows of $136bn):** Americas +$123bn, EMEA +$13bn, APAC ~$0. LTM: Americas +$490bn, EMEA +$192bn, APAC −$62bn (release). **Listed vs unlisted:** the overwhelming majority of AUM is listed/liquid (ETFs, index, public fixed income); unlisted is ≈ private markets at $320bn (~2.3% of AUM). **Aladdin:** ~$25T of assets on the platform (not extracted line by line from a primary source this cycle — see gaps).

| GIP (Global Infrastructure Partners) | 01.10.2024 | ~$12.55bn | $3bn cash + ~12m BLK shares | ~$170bn of infra AUM; ~$750m of run-rate fees (the run-rate is not verified) |

co.blackrock.sections.3.deep.0.body:
First, what takes the panic out. BLK is not facing insolvency: it is a capital-light, fee-only manager — the ~$15.34T of assets under management (AUM) at 30.06.2026 (+22% YoY, $12.53T → $15.34T) is CLIENTS' money, not BlackRock's balance sheet. FY2025 delivered $5,553m of GAAP net income on $24,216m of revenue; debt is token against the cash flow. The Q2 2026 report (released 15.07.2026) settled the main question on the operating trend: the adjusted operating margin reached 45.9% — an almost five-year high — against a through-cycle target of ≥45% (for comparison: 44.1% for full-year FY2025, 44.5% in Q1 2026). Inflows are at records: $868bn of net inflows over 12 months, a record $321bn in H1 2026 ($192bn in Q2), and organic base fee growth of 8% in Q2 (~10% LTM); iShares passed $6T. As an issuer, BLK is resilient.

But a resilient balance sheet is not the absence of risk, and the risk here sorts by origin into two groups worth holding apart:

**The fee base — what the AUM is tied to (positioning).** BLK's income is base management fees on AUM. ~55% of AUM ($7,661m, per the Q1 2026 disclosure) is equity, which falls almost 1:1 in a market drawdown and drags base fees with it. Inside that sits iShares, now past $6T: 44% of base fees on ~39% of AUM at a ~0.16% rate — the most profitable franchise and, simultaneously, the epicentre of a structural passive price war (Vanguard, State Street, Fidelity). Add the low-margin institutional index outflow (−$108bn over 12 months) as a signal on mandates.

**The business model — how the value is built.** Over 18 months BLK has spent ~$27bn on GIP, HPS and Preqin, pivoting into private markets and data. The risk here is integration and marks: earnout revaluations have already swung wildly — from a $455m charge (Q1'25) to a $549m gain (Q1'26) year on year (sequentially: a $96m charge in Q4'25 → a $549m gain in Q1'26, a swing of ~$645m); the GAAP operating margin fell to 29.1% in 2025 against 44.1% as-adjusted; and the deals were paid mostly in stock (dilution of +5% YoY to ~165m shares). To that add the antitrust common-ownership suit against the Big Three and the question of succession after Fink. This is a story about the multiple and about execution, not about a break: base fees and inflows are growing.

Each group is taken apart below: what it is, what supports it and what breaks it.

co.blackrock.sections.3.deep.1.items.0.d: BLK's income is base management fees on AUM, not its own assets. Two vulnerabilities meet in a single line. The first is market beta: equity is $7,661bn (55% of AUM, 48% of base fees, per the Q1 2026 disclosure) and falls almost 1:1 with the market — a 20% S&P 500 drawdown cuts that base with no outflow at all. The second is a structural price war: iShares passed $6T in Q2 2026 and delivers 44% of base fees on ~39% of AUM at an effective rate of ~0.16%; Vanguard, State Street and Fidelity push rates down. What softens it: the mix shift and the momentum — active plus private markets still deliver the lion's share of base fees, organic base fee growth was 8% in Q2 (≥5% for many consecutive quarters), and technology revenue (Aladdin) is $566m a quarter.

co.blackrock.sections.3.deep.4.body: Hold. Solvency is not in question — a capital-light, fee-only model with FY2025 net income of $5,553m — and the Q2 2026 report settled the main operating question: the as-adjusted margin reached 45.9% (an almost five-year high, against a ≥45% target), organic base fee growth was 8%, H1 inflows hit a record $321bn, iShares passed $6T, and as-adjusted EPS was $13.91 (+15% YoY) — the "margin ≥45% plus private markets inflows" trigger partly fired. The argument now is about the multiple (a forward P/E of ~19–20x, having recovered part of the de-rating, against ~22–23x historically), where the market pays grudgingly for three things: integration and marks in private markets after ~$27bn of deals, the passive price war through iShares (44% of base fees at a ~0.16% rate), and the regulatory overhang (the common-ownership suit, succession after Fink). Add if the Q3 2026 report confirms an as-adjusted margin ≥45% and net private markets inflows for another two consecutive quarters, with the multiple recovering. Reduce if the S&P 500 falls −20%+ (equity AUM of $7,661bn and base fees fall ~1:1), or if the Section 7 common-ownership suit advances, or if credit stress appears in HPS/HLEND: those are a permanent de-rating of the fee base and the private markets block, not a one-off episode.

**BlackRock** is the only manager combining four pieces that no peer has together: number one in the world in index/ETF (iShares >$6T, including the spot Bitcoin fund IBIT), a large active business, a fast-growing private markets arm (GIP/HPS/Preqin, $329bn of AUM, +$15.4bn of inflows in the quarter) and the Aladdin technology platform the whole industry runs on (technology revenue of $566m a quarter, +13% YoY, sold to competitors among others). Proof the model works: a 45.9% adjusted operating margin at $15.34T of scale — and that on the lowest effective fee in the group, ~14–15 bp (index drags it down): scale plus tech offsets the thin fee. The honest negative: percentage organic growth is slower than the pure alts', the 12-month return is the weakest of the four (+11.7% against Invesco's +77.6%), plus the political ESG backlash, the antitrust question over Big Three voting concentration and the open question of succession after Fink. The decision: **hold/add** — you pay for durability and the private markets option at a forward P/E of ~19–20x (after the Q2 bounce), not for the fastest growth; the trim signal is organic base fee growth falling below 5% with private markets inflows stalling.

**State Street** is second by AUM ($5.7T) and first in custody ($54.5T), but the economics are different: income is tied to rates, FX and custody volumes rather than alpha; the +39.6% over the year reflects a re-rating of the banking story, not the management one.

**Invesco** is the best performer (+77.6% over the year): record AUM of $2.47T and recovering flows around the QQQ ETF; but the story stands on one leg — concentration in a single flagship product.

**T. Rowe Price** has the highest fee (~40 bp) and margin (~46%), but sits structurally on the wrong side of the shift: the active strategies are losing money (−$13.7bn in the quarter), and −8.5% year to date makes it the only one in the red; the premium for active management is compressing.

co.blackrock.sections.6.deep.0.body: BlackRock is the world's largest asset manager: $15.34T of assets under management (AUM) at the end of Q2 2026 (+22% YoY). The thing that matters for valuation: that is CLIENTS' money, not BlackRock's balance sheet. The firm's own economics are not the appreciation of those assets but the fees on them: base management fees, performance fees, technology revenue (Aladdin) and private markets management. The model is capital-light: BlackRock does not risk its own capital but earns a percentage of other people's. That makes the size of AUM less important than its mix: 2% of assets in private markets deliver 11% of base fees (an effective rate of ~0.78%), while 28% of assets in institutional index deliver only 7% of fees (~0.03%). The entire strategy is shifting that mix towards high-margin products: iShares has passed $6T, the acquisitions of HPS (private credit, $150.9bn) and GIP (infrastructure, $113.5bn) build the private markets block, and Aladdin delivers recurring revenue that does not depend on the market. The metric management judges itself by is not headline AUM but organic base fee growth: 8% in Q2 and 10% over the last 12 months, against a 5% target.

co.blackrock.sections.7.bodyMarkdown:
**What they believe (quotes from Fink's letter of 23.03.2026 as relayed by the secondary source Semafor; the original blackrock.com PDF returns 403, so not checked verbatim):**
- "Self-reliance is costly" — economies are making a hawkish turn and investors will have to put more money to work at home; private capital has to close the gaps in AI, energy and defence.
- "There's a real risk artificial intelligence could widen wealth inequality if ownership does not broaden" — hence broadening retail access to private and early-stage AI assets.
- AI/cloud/electrification = demand for infrastructure (the "$1.5T into data centres by 2030" thesis, Investor Day); BlackRock is top-3 in infrastructure through GIP.
- A shift from 60/40 to 50/30/20 with 20% in private assets (the 2026 Private Markets Outlook).
- The 401(k) as a channel into private assets — Fink supports admitting unlisted assets into retirement accounts.

**What they avoid:** they left Climate Action 100+ and the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative (against the backdrop of the states' antitrust suit under a common ownership theory). Cash management is not a growth priority (low margin, despite $1,073bn of AUM).

**What they are watching:** asset-based finance and private high-grade credit (a "profound increase" in opportunities in 2026, per the 2026 Private Markets Outlook); international and EM equities (the driver of Q1 2026 iShares inflows); tokenisation and digital assets.

co.blackrock.sections.9.bodyMarkdown:
> Below are the analyst's conclusions, NOT quotes from filings. Not a valuation: no DCF and no fair value estimates.

**What the recent events mean.**
- The engine is running steadily: Q1 2026 delivered $130bn of inflows, 8% organic base fee growth (a seventh consecutive quarter at ≥5%, 10% LTM) and an as-adjusted margin of 44.5% (+130 bp). The organic growth is no longer a one-off. iShares ($132bn of inflows, 44% of base fees on 39% of AUM) is the main source of predictability.
- M&A is moving from "cost" to "income": GIP/HPS/Preqin hit GAAP in 2025 (EPS $35.31, −16% YoY on non-cash items), but as-adjusted EPS was $48.09 (+10%). 2026 is the first full year of the combined platform; HPS delivered $121m of performance fees in Q1 2026, and GIP V is majority committed. The signal: the GAAP/adjusted gap will narrow as the one-off charges disappear — but the contingent consideration line is volatile in both directions (Q1'26 produced a +$549m gain), so it must be normalised in every release.
- The $400bn private markets target by 2030 is the main checkable KPI. Slowing fundraising or problem loans at HPS/HLEND would hurt the thesis more than swings in AUM.

**Context for a BLK holder.** BLK is a proxy for (a) rising markets (55% of AUM in equity → beta to the indices), (b) ETF inflows (structural) and (c) the expansion of private credit (cyclical risk). Holding BLK already gives an investor diversified fee-based access to markets; a separate broad index position partly duplicates it, and a direct private credit position doubles down on the same cycle. Antitrust risk (common ownership) is systemic across the whole BLK/Vanguard/State Street trio.

**Signals (triggers, not a recommendation):**
- HOLD/ADD: organic base fee growth ≥5%; as-adjusted margin ≥45%; ETF inflows ≥~$100bn a quarter; private markets fundraising running at ~$65–80bn a year (what $400bn by 2030 requires).
- TRIM: organic base fee growth below 5% for two consecutive quarters; rising impairments or contingent consideration on HPS-GIP signalling overpayment; problem loans at HLEND (watch non-accruals in the BDC's 10-Q); Fink or Kapito selling faster than their usual rhythm.
- WATCH (not a trade): the motion to dismiss in the antitrust suit is denied → revisit the whole passive complex.

**The AI lens (where it is real):** directly, through infrastructure for data centres and electrification (GIP) and through broadening retail access to early-stage AI companies. GIP genuinely owns power and data centre infrastructure, so the lens is not a stretch. For core asset management the AI lens is secondary.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.0.body: BlackRock is a bet that the world's money flows to the broadest and cheapest manager. Assets under management (AUM) of $15.34T (30.06.2026, +22% YoY) is CLIENTS' money, a fee base, not BlackRock's balance sheet. The model is capital-light: income comes from fees, not from its own investments. The thesis rests on three parts: (1) scale and inflows — a record $868bn of net inflows over 12 months at 10% organic base fee growth (8% in Q2), with iShares past $6T; (2) the shift into a higher-margin mix — private markets are 2% of AUM ($329bn) but 11% of base fees ($639m), and the adjusted operating margin of 45.9% is an almost five-year high; (3) a de-rating on record results — a forward P/E of ~17.7x against 22–23x historically (−21% from the 52-week peak of $1,220, source stockanalysis.com), plus a private markets and technology option not in the price (GIP ~$170bn of infrastructure, HPS ~$157bn of private credit, Preqin plus Aladdin) and the 2030 target of revenue above $35bn with $400bn of private markets fundraising.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essence
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.1.body: Beta risk: 55% of AUM ($7.66T) is equity, so the fee base moves almost 1:1 with the market, and an S&P slump hits revenue directly. The passive price war: iShares/ETFs are 39–41% of AUM but base fees there are ~0.16% — constant price pressure. Index outflows: institutional index is −$108bn over 12 months (−$41bn in Q2) — money leaving a segment that already pays little (28% of AUM delivers just 7% of fees). Integration risk: GIP + HPS + Preqin (~$27bn of deals) have already diluted the shares by +5%, and contingent consideration revaluations swing (−$96m in Q4'25 → +$549m in Q1'26). Carry is a promise, not a fact: performance fees jump around ($754m in Q4'25 → $272m in Q1'26 → $305m in Q2'26), and sustained conversion from private markets is still unproven. Regulation and governance: the common-ownership (Section 7) suit and the open question of succession after Fink. The market wants proof that the 45.9% margin and $868bn of inflows will hold rather than reverse on the first market fall.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.2.items.0.d: Q2 2026 has already confirmed the bull case: an adjusted margin of 45.9% (clearing the ≥45% threshold), organic base fee growth of 8%, AUM of $15.34T. Private markets convert carry, and HPS/GIP grow fee-paying AUM. iShares stays above $6T and keeps growing, with inflows for a second consecutive quarter. The P/E returns to 20–22x on record results. The $2bn 2026 buyback runs below intrinsic value. The 2030 target: revenue above $35bn and $400bn of private markets fundraising.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.2.items.1.d: The S&P falls 20% — the fee base (55% in equity, $7.66T) falls almost 1:1. Rates stay higher for longer and private markets inflows freeze, leaving carry on paper. The price war compresses iShares' yield. GIP/HPS integration stalls and volatile contingent consideration revaluations hit GAAP earnings (a 34.7% GAAP margin against 45.9% adjusted). The common-ownership suit advances. The P/E stays at ~17x and no re-rating happens.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.2.title: Two scenarios
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.3.items.0.v: Hold the position. The add trigger has already partly fired: the Q2 2026 adjusted margin of 45.9% (≥45%) alongside 8% organic base fee growth. Add on confirmation of private markets inflows for a second consecutive quarter, or on a pullback below $850 (a P/E under 16x). Reduce on: the S&P falling 20%, the common-ownership suit advancing, credit stress at HPS/HLEND, or organic base fee growth below 5% YoY — which would mean the machine is losing market share.
co.blackrock.sections.9.deep.3.items.1.v: Mid-October 2026 — the Q3 report (the test: the margin holds ≥45%, organic growth ≥5%, and watch institutional index at −$41bn in Q2). H2 2026 — the general launch of Aladdin on AWS. The dividend of $5.73/quarter (+10%) — not confirmed against a primary source, awaiting the Q1 2026 8-K. Investor Day: the 2030 targets (>$35bn of revenue, $400bn of private markets).

co.blackrock.summary: BlackRock manages $13.89T of other people's money and lives on the fees, not on its own balance sheet. Two engines: iShares — the world's largest ETF range (41% of assets but 45% of fees, now past $6T) — and private markets: 2% of assets but 11% of fees plus almost all of the performance fees. Plus Aladdin, software with durable subscription revenue. After ~$27bn of acquisitions (GIP, HPS, Preqin) the money is flowing into private credit and AI infrastructure. Inflows this year are at a record and the margin is 45.9%. The risk: 58% of assets are equities, so in a market crash the fees fall with the market.
co.blackrock.tagline: BlackRock is the world's largest asset manager ($13.89T of AUM): its income is fees on the assets it manages, and the economics are driven by iShares ETFs (44% of base fees) and, since GIP/HPS/Preqin, by high-margin private markets. The hold/add/cut decision rests on converting record inflows ($744bn LTM) into base and performance fees at an as-adjusted margin above 45%; meanwhile the stock sits near its 52-week low and below its historical forward P/E.

co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.3.det: This is not a one-off deal but a pipeline: every new data centre in the programme is an order for BEP's power and BIP's infrastructure. Together with the Microsoft contract, it is the main confirmation of Brookfield's AI thesis in real capital.

An umbrella investment programme (launched 19.11.2025): Brookfield and its partners are assembling up to $100bn of assets across the whole AI chain — power plants, data centres and fibre networks. NVIDIA participates as technology partner, and the Kuwait Investment Authority — one of the world's largest sovereign funds — as lead investor. co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.3.tit: AI Infrastructure Program — the programme with NVIDIA and Kuwait's sovereign fund
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.3.why: A long-term programme: building generation, data centres and fibre specifically for AI. A multi-year pipeline of projects for BEP and BIP.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.4.det: Where it sits in the portfolio
A typical BBU deal: a niche manufacturer with steady repeat sales. Not an AI story — simply predictable cash flow.

Antylia Scientific makes laboratory consumables: instruments, single-use materials, water testing kits. Its customers are pharma, biotech and environmental labs that buy continuously, regardless of the economic cycle. The deal price was not disclosed.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.4.tit: Antylia Scientific — an acquisition with CDPQ
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.4.why: A maker of laboratory equipment and consumables (pharma, biotech, water testing). Bought by the private equity arm (BBU) alongside the Canadian pension fund CDPQ.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.5.det: Where it sits in the portfolio
It extends BIP's digital infrastructure (towers plus data centres plus fibre) into a growing market. The logic is the same as in the AI programme: own the pipes the traffic runs through.

The tower business is simple: one tower is leased to several mobile operators at once, and they pay for years — moving a tower is expensive and pointless. India is one of the fastest-growing mobile internet markets in the world. The amount and structure of the deal were not disclosed.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.5.tit: American Tower India — an investor group buys the telecom towers
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.5.why: BIP and its partners are buying American Tower's Indian business — a portfolio of telecom towers. Towers rent space to mobile operators for a recurring fee.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.6.det: The Brookfield model in action: build or buy → raise the value → sell the mature asset → put the money into something new at a higher return. Selling at a good price confirms their asset marks are not inflated.
Saeta Yield is a Spanish portfolio of 745 MW of operating solar plants. Brookfield sold it to Masdar — Abu Dhabi's state energy company, which buys completed green assets worldwide.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.6.why: Selling a mature solar portfolio: the assets are built and have appreciated — the money is recycled into new X-Elio projects at higher returns.
co.brookfield.changesDeep.timeline.7.det: An exit from a mature asset at full price. The fund's profit is crystallised — meaning Brookfield receives fund profits in cash, not on paper.
Patrick Terminals is Australia's largest container port operator, which BIP had owned for years. Sold to a buyer group for A$2.5bn — a full exit.

co.brookfield.sections.3.bodyMarkdown:
BN's risk is not that the business breaks. The company is resilient: 95% of the debt is non-recourse to the holdco, and maturities to 2030 are covered by cash on hand. But the risk is not singular — it arrives from three different directions.

| Risk | Direction | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Debt and refinancing | how it is financed | 95% of the debt sits at the assets; if rates rise or an asset weakens, BN's stake in it gets cheaper — no bankruptcy required |
| AI infrastructure concentration | what the money is in | a bet on power and data centres (a $200bn pipeline); disappointment in AI returns and a capex squeeze hit the whole infrastructure book at once |
| Two marks — carry and insurance | how the value is counted | $60bn+ is valued by management itself (10x and 15x); the market pays zero for both |

At $44.08 the market is already priced where the valuation sits with carry and the insurance franchise written to zero — it is not paying for those marks. But that is only one of the three risks; the credit and asset risks need looking at separately.
co.brookfield.sections.3.deep.0.body:
First, what takes the panic out. BN is not facing bankruptcy: 95% of the debt ($249.5bn) sits against specific assets with no recourse to the holdco, and five years of maturities are already covered by cash on hand. In 2023 the group handed its Los Angeles towers, ~$1.1bn, back to the banks — and the loss stopped at fund level, never reaching the holdco. As a whole, the company is resilient.

But resilience is not the same as the absence of risk, and the risk here is not singular. It arrives from three different directions, and they are worth holding apart:

**How the company is financed.** Almost all the debt sits at the assets themselves. If rates rise or an asset weakens, refinancing gets more expensive, capital has to be injected into the asset, and BN's stake in it gets cheaper — no bankruptcy required.

**What the money is invested in.** Brookfield is betting heavily on AI infrastructure — power and data centres, a $200bn pipeline. If AI returns disappoint and hyperscaler capex contracts, the blow lands across the whole infrastructure and power book at once, not on a single asset.

**How the value is counted.** 59% of the assets ($102.8bn of $175.3bn) are marked by management itself; two of the large marks — future fund profits (carry) and the insurance franchise — the market does not recognise at all.

Each is taken apart below: what it is, what supports it and what breaks it.
co.brookfield.sections.3.deep.0.title: The thesis: no bankruptcy — but the risk is not singular
Of the group's $249.5bn of debt, only 5% ($14.3bn) has recourse to the holding company itself — which protects against bankruptcy, not against losses. The mechanism is quiet: a weak asset or higher rates → interest cover falls → refinancing costs more → capital has to be injected into the asset → BN's stake in it gets cheaper. No bankruptcy required. Today the position is healthy: maturities to 2030 ($3.66bn) are covered by cash on hand ($5.48bn), and the debt is long and fixed — 15 years, 4.8%, with 74% maturing after 2031.

The weak spot: on that 95% of the debt Brookfield discloses neither interest cover, nor a maturity schedule, nor the floating-rate share — it cannot be checked, and that is exactly where the shareholder's risk lives.

HEADLINE: there are NO individual Form 4 filings in the SEC for purchases or sales of BN or BAM stock by senior management — and that is a structural fact, not a data gap (see below). The insider-confidence signal here is read not through Form 4 but through corporate actions: the buyback ($1bn+ YTD), the dividend increase (+17%) and the large personal holdings disclosed in the proxy.

**Form 4 / Section 16 — why there are no personal transactions**

BN and BAM are Canadian foreign private issuers (BN is incorporated in Ontario and headquartered in Toronto; its SEC category is large accelerated filer, forms 40-F/6-K). Their officers and directors are exempt from Section 16 and do NOT file Form 4 with the SEC for transactions in BN/BAM stock. Personal insider transactions are disclosed in Canada's SEDI system, and aggregate ownership in the annual Management Information Circular (proxy). That is why openinsider returns an empty table for the BN ticker (which its database maps to the delisted Banta Corp), and nothing with an issuer for BAM; openinsider/SEC Form 4 are uninformative for this company (checked: empty output).

IMPORTANT — reclassifying the previous claim: the 175 Form 4 filings under CIK BN (0001001085) and 10 under CIK BAM (0001937926) turn out, on parsing the XML, NOT to be transactions in BN/BAM stock but reports by BN/BAM as 10%+ owners of the non-traded **Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust** (Brookfield REIT) they manage. These are routine Class I subscriptions and redemptions at a NAV of ~$10.4 (code J), not trading in their own shares. The specific lines (SEC EDGAR Form 4, opened and parsed line by line):

| Transaction date | Filer | Issuer | Code | Buy/Sell | Shares | Price (NAV) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18.06.2026 | Brookfield Corp | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A (acquired) | 107,584 | $10.3874 |
| 20.05.2026 | Brookfield Corp | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A | 105,468 | $10.3689 |
| 20.04.2026 | Brookfield Corp | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A | 105,505 | $10.3726 |
| 31.03.2026 | Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | D (disposed) | 314,545 | $10.3726 |
| 20.02.2026 | Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. | Brookfield REIT, Class I | J | A | 105,895 | $10.3778 |

The previous claim — "Bruce Flatt, Form 4 of 28.02.2026, ~107m shares, uninformative buy" — is withdrawn: the Form 4 nearest that date (filed 24.02.2026) is a BAM subscription into Brookfield REIT, not a Flatt transaction in BN stock. No personal Flatt Form 4 exists at the SEC (foreign private issuer).

**Management ownership (BN 2025 Management Information Circular, primary IR PDF, extracted with pdfplumber)**
- **Bruce Flatt (CEO):** holds **18,018,523** Class A and Exchangeable Class A shares directly and indirectly (note k of the circular). The widely quoted "~107–142m shares" from aggregators is NOT personal ownership but the block controlled through the Partners' collective vehicles (see below).
- **The Class B control block.** At 17.04.2025 BN had 1,647,462,652 Class A and just 85,120 Class B Limited Voting Shares (all privately held). The Class B shares sit in a trust; beneficial and voting interests are split one third each between Bruce Flatt, Jack L. Cockwell and, jointly, the five Partners (Kingston, Lawson, Madon, Pollock, Shah). The circular says verbatim: "no single individual or entity controls the Trust". Through the Class B shares (which elect half the board) the Partners hold strategic control on a small economic stake.
- **Partners Value Investments L.P. (PVI):** the Partners' listed partnership owns **~121m** BN Class A, ~31m BAM Class A and ~8m BWS Class A (fully diluted); the Partners hold ≥90% of PVI's units (circular). What it means for the decision: management's interests are firmly aligned with BN over the long run — large personal and collective capital in the stock, with no sales recorded.

**Buybacks (the corporate undervaluation signal)**
- **BN:** $470m repurchased YTD at ~$41 on average (≈37% below management's $66.37 estimate); over 12 months, 23.0m shares at a weighted average of $38.75 — confirmed in the Supplemental (p.8).
- **BAM:** $575m repurchased — confirmed in the 8-K/Supplemental. Together, BN+BAM is **>$1bn YTD**.
- **NCIB (mechanics, primary).** The TSX approved the renewal of BN's normal course issuer bid over **191,034,672** Class A shares = 10% of the public float; the period runs **27.05.2026–26.05.2027**; the daily TSX limit is 722,889 shares (25% of ADTV); purchases may be made on the TSX/NYSE/ATS; repurchased shares are cancelled or held in trust for the LTIP; an automatic purchase plan runs from mid-June 2026 (announced 25.05.2026). So the buyback is not a one-off but a renewable mandate.

**Dividend / share issuance**
- **BN:** the quarterly dividend was raised from $0.06 to **$0.07** per Class A share (an annual rate of **$0.28**, ≈+17%) — declared in February 2026, paid 31.03.2026 and 30.06.2026 (IR distributions page, opened). There have been no cuts; the policy remains a "modest dividend" with reinvestment through buybacks. Raising it in a year when the stock sits in the lower-middle of its annual range is a supportive signal.
- **BAM:** announced "record 2025 results and 15% dividend increase" (BAM IR press release; the headline was confirmed by web search, but the exact quarterly dividend of $0.5025 comes from an aggregator and was not re-opened against the primary source in this check — see gaps).
- **Preferred reset (06.2026):** BN fixed the reset rate on its Series 24 preference shares at 5.432% a year ($0.3395/quarter) for five years from 01.07.2026, with a right to convert into floating Series 25 (4.623% annualised); 10,808,027 Series 24 shares are outstanding — confirmed in BN's 6-K of 01.06.2026 (opened). This concerns the preferreds, not the Class A.
- **The BN+BWS merger** (26.05.2026): a 1-for-1 exchange, Brookfield Corporation Ltd., NYSE/TSX, tax-deferred, vote 16.07.2026 — confirmed by GlobeNewswire. Effect on the share count: BWS class A exchangeable shares convert 1-for-1 into BN.
- **BAM senior notes** (subsequent): $1.0bn ($550m @ 4.832% + $450m @ 5.298%) plus a $1.0bn CP programme — confirmed in the 8-K.

**Reading it for the decision (hold/add/cut).** There are by definition no personal Form 4 insider buys here, so we lean on corporate proxies: (1) a $1bn+ YTD buyback at ~$41 against management's $66.37 estimate — management clearly thinks the stock is cheap; (2) a +17% dividend increase; (3) very large personal and collective Partner ownership (Flatt personally ~18.0m Class A; PVI ~121m BN Class A) with no recorded sales. All three vectors point pro-hold/add. There is no value-destructive spin-off or issuance; the BN+BWS merger is 1-for-1 and non-dilutive. The structural drawback for tracking: personal insider transactions cannot be monitored through the SEC — only through SEDI (Canada).

We compare BN's management business (i.e. BAM) against the largest alternative managers. Every peer figure has been re-opened against the primary SEC 8-Ks (KKR, BX, APO — EDGAR; aggregators are no longer used).

| Metric | BAM (Brookfield) | Blackstone (BX) | Apollo (APO) | KKR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRE, quarter | $772m (+11%) | $1,548m (+23%) | $728m (+30%) | $1,016m (+24%) |
| Total AUM | >$1.0T | $1.30T | $1.03T | $758bn |
| Fee-paying AUM | $614bn (+12%) | $937.6bn | $836bn (FGAUM) | $615bn (+17%) |

**Important: the row above is FRE (fee-related earnings), not management fees.** It was previously labelled "fees": the figures are correct and comparable (FRE against FRE), but the label was wrong. Actual quarterly management fees are markedly higher — BX $2,133m, KKR $1,193m, APO ~$1.0bn, BAM $990m (consolidated).

Confirmed against the primary SEC 8-Ks: KKR — FRE $1,016m (+24%), AUM $758bn (+14%), fee-bearing capital $615bn (+17%). BX — FRE $1,548m (+23%), AUM $1.30T, fee-earning $937.6bn (BX labels all its Q1'26 figures "preliminary and unaudited"). APO — FRE $728m (+30%), AUM $1.03T, FGAUM $836bn.

⚠️ **These companies count AUM differently, and it is not directly comparable:** Apollo's AUM includes the Athene insurance balance sheet ($401bn ≈ 39% of AUM), and KKR's includes Global Atlantic ($220bn ≈ 29%). BX counts most conservatively. FRE is the only row in the table that is pre-tax for all of them and therefore genuinely comparable.

**Positioning:**
- **FRE size/pace:** BAM ($772m, +11%) trails BX and KKR in absolute terms and grows the slowest of the four (APO +30%, KKR +24%, BX +23%).
- **Capital mix:** BAM has the heaviest hard-asset tilt — $282bn of credit plus real assets (infrastructure/power/real estate) against BX's broader PE/credit mix and Apollo's insurance tilt.
- **What is unique to BN:** unlike the pure managers, a BN investor also gets direct capital in BIP/BEP/BBUC/BPG, carry on the balance sheet ($6.4bn net) and insurance (WS $30.4bn) — diversification that dilutes the purity of the fee-stream story.
- **Conclusion for the decision:** on fee-business growth BAM lags its peers, but BN offers upside through the discount to management's estimate ($66 vs ~$43), carry realisation and the Westinghouse option, none of which the peers have. The hold/add case rests on BN's discount and its optionality, not on BAM leading on FRE growth.

co.brookfield.sections.5.deep.3.body:
**Brookfield** is the only owner-operator in the group: ~85,000 employees physically run assets, not money. Five names it is built from: **Westinghouse** (nuclear power), **Compass** (data centres), **Oaktree** (credit), **Clarios** (an operating business) and **Canary Wharf** (real estate). Its competitors manage capital — and a 10.5 GW contract for Microsoft cannot be delivered with a cheque; the generation has to be built and commissioned. The price of that: the slowest fee growth of the group (+11% against +23–30% for peers) and the worst AUM monetisation (61% against 72–81%). But that same slowness creates the ~35% discount to management's own estimate, and the hold case is that its operating edge in electrification closes it.

**Blackstone** is the largest by scale ($1.30T of AUM) and the most efficient at converting AUM into fees (72%). Its edge: an asset-light model that scales without freezing capital. Over 12 months it has quietly rebuilt its mix — 35% of AUM is now credit and insurance rather than classic real estate and buyout. The legacy: the BXMT mortgage REIT carries ~7% past due and pays dividends out of principal — not the main business, but an indicator that Blackstone has not fully exited the commercial property cycle.

**Apollo** grows fastest (+30% fees YoY) through one powerful channel: the Athene insurance arm raises its own capital through annuities, deploys it into loans ($71bn a quarter) and pays Apollo the fees on it. That closed loop delivers speed — and it is also first in line for the NAIC's 2026 review of capital requirements. If the regulator tightens the rules, growth stops abruptly rather than gradually, because there is only one channel.

**KKR** is the most diversified: private equity 30%, credit 43%, insurance through Global Atlantic, plus $18.3bn of deferred earnings in Strategic Holdings (direct balance sheet investments). On half Blackstone's AUM ($758bn) it monetises just as efficiently (81%) — earning a third more fees than Brookfield off the same base ($615bn against $614bn). The risk: its insurance channel runs the same model as Apollo's Athene — a regulatory hit to one touches both.

Neither Blackstone nor Apollo nor KKR has all of those pieces in-house — they would have to buy them in and share the profit with partners. The same linkage speeds up deals: when Brookfield buys an asset it immediately installs its own operators, refinances through its own credit and holds it on permanent capital — a closed loop. The other side of that: Brookfield is structurally behind in credit, buyout PE and tech, and over five years its stock has trailed KKR (~28%) and Apollo (~21%) with its own ~12%. The hold case: the ability to carry a full infrastructure project single-handed closes the ~35% discount.

The investment committee thinks almost entirely about not losing. Target returns: 6–8% in a bad case, 12–15% in a normal one, 20%+ in a good one. Every asset is financed separately — one asset's debt cannot drag the others down.

Management values the company at $66.37 a share while the market pays ~$42.87 — a discount of about 35% (and management itself has been buying stock back at that same ~$41). That is the whole thesis: we are buying below what the company says it is worth. If the gap narrows towards 20% the bet pays off; if it widens past 45% while fees keep growing, buying gets more attractive still.
$11.8bn of fund profits are accrued on paper, but only $528m turned into actual cash over the last year. The market simply does not believe the paper will become cash — hence the entire discount. If the flow accelerates to $1.5–2bn a year the thesis is confirmed and it is worth adding; if it stays flat, the market is right not to pay for carry.
Fees are the group's most stable and most valuable income: $772m in the quarter (+11% YoY) and $3.1bn for the year (+18%). Healthy means growth of at least 11% a year. The moment fee-bearing capital grows below 8%, the machine is slowing — and that is a signal to reduce.
The company sold $17bn of assets in the quarter "at or above carrying values" — which proves the balance sheet marks are real rather than drawn. As long as sales clear at the marks, the balance sheet can be trusted; once assets start selling at a discount to it, the whole valuation comes into question.
The company may repurchase up to 191m shares (10% of the free float) over a year and has already spent $470m on BN (~$41 a share) and $575m on BAM. If management is buying, management thinks the stock is cheap. Accelerating the buyback at a low price is a strong signal; stopping it is a reason to take notice.
In the US the company does not disclose its executives' personal transactions (foreign private issuer); they appear only in Canada's SEDI database at sedi.ca. Large sales by executives are an early warning. So far the corporate signal points the other way: buybacks are running and the dividend was raised 17%.

co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.0.body: Brookfield is a bet that the physical world is worth more than the digital one. While the market pays 30-40x for a SaaS subscription, Brookfield buys the power plants, ports and data centres without which that SaaS does not run. $1T under management, $175bn of its own assets, 250,000 people on site — not a fund but an operator on the scale of a state. The thesis stands on three legs: a ~35% discount to management's own valuation (>$1bn of buybacks year to date at ~$41 — management thinks the stock is cheap), $11.8bn of unrealised fund profits (which turn into cash as assets are sold — $91bn was sold over the year at or above carrying values), and an AI/power option that is not in the price ($200bn of data centres, Westinghouse with the only licensed reactor in the US, the 10.5 GW Microsoft contract).
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.0.title: The essence
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.1.body: Concentration: 55-59% of BN's value is the management company plus future fund profits. A blow to one hits both. BAM's fees grow more slowly than peers' (+11% against APO +30%, KKR +24%). The insurance business is at the margin (a 99% combined ratio), and after the BN+BWS merger any losses move onto the parent balance sheet. The $11.8bn of carry is a promise, not a fact: only $528m turned into cash over 12 months. The main reason for the discount is that BN's accounting profit is falling ~35% a year on paper revaluations of buildings and funds. The multi-listing structure (BN, BAM, BIP, BEP) puts investors off — the market wants proof that fund profits become cash rather than staying on paper.
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.1.title: What stands in the way, and why the market disagrees
The merger is approved on 16.07.2026 and the discount narrows towards 20%. Carry starts converting: $2-3bn over 12 months instead of $528m. The AI programme lands its first construction contracts. The DOE documents the loan and Westinghouse re-rates towards $30bn+. Buybacks continue below intrinsic value. Flatt holds 18m shares personally, PVI 121m.
Rates stay higher for longer and asset sales freeze. Carry stays on paper for another 2-3 years. BAM loses share: fundraising slows and fee growth falls below 10%. The insurance business burns capital (a combined ratio above 100%). Westinghouse is a good business, but without new reactors it is not a transformation. The $26.9bn of real estate is marked down. Total DE keeps falling.
co.brookfield.sections.9.deep.2.title: Two scenarios
Hold the position as a single line through BN (which already contains the stake in the BAM management company). Add on: a discount above 40% (a price below $40), or a quarter with carry accelerating after the BN+BWS merger closes; BAM fee growth of +15%+ YoY confirms the picture. Reduce on: an insurance combined ratio above 100%, or BAM fee-bearing capital growth below 8% YoY — which would mean the machine is losing market share.
16.07.2026 — the BN+BWS vote (the key one). 06.08.2026 — the Q2 report (the test: fees above $3.1bn over 12 months, carry accelerating). 2026 — DOE definitive financing for Westinghouse

co.brookfield.summary: Brookfield Corporation (BN) is the world's largest owner of real infrastructure. It manages ~$1T through funds and owns $175bn of assets outright: power plants, ports, data centres, real estate, pipelines. 250,000 employees run those assets directly — this is an operator, not just a fund. Fees are $3.1bn/yr (+18%). The main bets: AI infrastructure (a $200bn pipeline), nuclear power (Westinghouse) and private credit (Oaktree). It trades at a ~35% discount to management's own valuation.
co.brookfield.tagline: BN is the parent holding company: its stake in BAM plus accrued fund profits make up ~59% of asset value; the market holds it at a ~35% discount to management's own estimate ($66.37 vs ~$43).
co.brookfield.topBets.items.0.fact: It builds reactors and services operating nuclear plants for decades — a continuous income stream (co-owned with Cameco). The bet: only nuclear supplies round-the-clock clean electricity, and AI and data centres need ever more of it.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.1.fact: It builds vast data campuses on long leases to Microsoft and other giants — contracted money, not speculation. The bet: own the buildings AI runs in, rather than guess which AI company wins.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.2.fact: $209bn under management; the profile is distressed debt (the legendary Howard Marks), and earnings rise precisely in a crisis. The bet: private credit is replacing the banks and is the group's fastest-growing business.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.3.fact: Its battery is in one car in three worldwide, petrol and electric alike; ~80% of sales are replacements. The bet: steady cash flow that Brookfield makes more efficient.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.4.fact: 20m+ sq ft of offices and housing in London; Brookfield is reworking a district hit by remote working into housing and laboratories. The bet: quality property in a top location recovers.
co.brookfield.topBets.items.4.role: A business district in central London

co.brookfield.verdict.rationale: A quality portfolio of real assets plus a growing management franchise, trading at a ~35% discount to management's own estimate — the asymmetry favours the upside.
co.brookfield.verdict.trigger: Add if the discount deepens past 40% or if the realisation of fund profits is confirmed; reduce if debt with recourse to BN rises or monetisations stall.
